newsitem.title: UK: Abbey National recovers post-results losses.
newsitem.headline: Abbey National recovers post-results losses.

text.p: Shares in British bank Abbey National Plc recovered their early losses on Tuesday, bouncing back from an initial post-results slide as investors focused on respectable headline profit growth, dealers said.
Abbey National shares were up four pence to 814 by 0935 GMT, having been as low as 789-3/4 in the immediate aftermath of the company's first-half results statement.

Although analysts said the dividend and market share figures were slightly disappointing, most said they were reasonably satisfied with the 23-percent rise in half-year pre-tax profits to 687 million stg, after a charge of 67 million relating to changes in the proposed rate of corporation tax.

"There are a few disappointments in there but overall the figures were fairly good and Abbey could still be a bid target," one market-maker said. "The results were reasonable, although not brilliant."
Analysts had forecast profits between 673 and 700 million and a dividend of between 10.2 and 10.5 pence.

"Although the numbers overall look okay, I think the dividend will be perceived as disappointing," said Panmure Gordon analyst David Poutney. "People were looking for an increase of 20 percent and it's gone up 17. Given that their tier 1 ratio has gone up from 8.5 to 9.2, that's disappointing."

Abbey National's market share of UK mortgages was estimated at 14.3 percent at June 30, up from 12.1 percent at the half-year stage the previous year but down from the full-year 1996 figure of 14.7 percent.

"The share of the mortgage market is really important given the conditions in the sector over the last year. People were looking for around 15 percent," one dealer said. "People want to see how much business Abbey held onto in what has been a very competitive year."
Poutney pointed out that margins were being squeezed.
"Margins are under pressure, although there's no great surprise there," he said. "So there's margin pressure plus loss of market share."
